paragraphs.heading: Coiled cousins of the octopus
paragraphs.text: Ammonoids are extinct cephalopods, animals that usually lived in a coiled shell, grouped together as the subclass Ammonoidea. Their shells look like those of nautiluses, yet their closer kin are octopuses, squid and cuttlefish. People often call them ammonites, a name used most for the order Ammonitida, the last group of them left from the Jurassic until they died out. More than 10,000 species have been described.

paragraphs.heading: Horns of a god
paragraphs.text: The name comes from the spiral of the fossil shells, which looks a bit like a tightly curled ram's horn. Pliny the Elder called these fossils ammonis cornua, the horns of Ammon, because the Egyptian god Ammon was usually shown wearing ram's horns. The horn idea lives on in scientific names: many ammonite genus names end in -ceras, from the Greek word for horn.

paragraphs.heading: A shell of rooms
paragraphs.text: The part of the shell divided into chambers is called the phragmocone. Its chambers, called camerae, get bigger and bigger along the coil and are separated by thin walls called septa. The living animal sat only in the last and largest room, the body chamber. As it grew, it built new, larger chambers onto the open end of the coil. Scientists sort ammonoids partly by the shape and decoration of these septa.

paragraphs.heading: Reading a lost way of life
paragraphs.text: Because ammonites are gone, we know little about how they lived, and their soft bodies are almost never preserved in any detail. Even so, researchers have learned a lot by studying the shells and by testing models of them in water tanks. Many species seem to have been filter feeders. Most shells are flat spirals, but some, called heteromorphs, are twisted like a corkscrew or not coiled at all, and these turn up mainly in the Cretaceous.

paragraphs.heading: Surviving one disaster after another
paragraphs.text: The first ammonoids appeared in the Early Devonian, around 410 to 408 million years ago. Again and again they came close to vanishing. The Hangenberg Event at the end of the Devonian left only a handful of lineages, and the end-Permian extinction pushed them to the edge once more. After the end-Triassic extinction only a few genera of one family survived, yet these gave rise to all later ammonites, which then branched out explosively in the Early Jurassic.

paragraphs.heading: The final blow
paragraphs.text: Ammonites stayed varied right to the end: at least 57 widespread species were alive in the last 500,000 years of the Cretaceous. All of them died out during or soon after the K-Pg extinction, which was caused by the Chicxulub impact. One idea is that the impact made the oceans more acidic, harming ammonite young, which were probably small and drifted as plankton. Nautiluses are thought to have laid eggs in small batches many times over their lives, on the sea floor and away from the strike's direct effects, so they made it through.

paragraphs.heading: Clocks in the rock
paragraphs.text: Ammonoids make excellent index fossils: finding a particular species or genus lets geologists tie that rock layer to a specific span of geologic time. They also came in a huge range of sizes. The smallest, Maximites, reached only 10 mm across as an adult. One of the largest known, Parapuzosia seppenradensis from Cretaceous Germany, sometimes measured 2 m across.
